sources.title: OSCAL: Open Security Controls Assessment Language
findings: OSCAL is a NIST-led effort with industry that offers open machine-readable formats in XML, JSON, and YAML to automate security and compliance work.
sources.limits: Landing page; the model details are on the layer page.

sources.title: OSCAL layers and models
findings: The control layer holds the catalog (a framework's controls) and the profile (a selected and tailored baseline).
The implementation layer holds component definitions and the system security plan, which records how a system implements controls.
The assessment layer holds the assessment plan, assessment results (findings, evidence, scope), and the plan of action and milestones for findings to fix.
sources.limits: Describes the data models, not whether a target or assessor accepts them.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Security and Privacy Controls
findings: The publication is a catalog of security and privacy controls in 20 families, applied within organization-wide risk management.
It separates functionality (strength of control mechanisms) from assurance (confidence that the control delivers the capability).
sources.limits: Abstract page only; the full catalog was not read.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-53B Control Baselines
findings: Provides low, moderate, and high impact security baselines and a privacy baseline.
Gives tailoring guidance for control selection and describes overlays that adapt baselines to a community, technology, or environment.
sources.limits: Abstract page only; written for US federal agencies.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-137 Information Security Continuous Monitoring
findings: A continuous monitoring program gives ongoing visibility of assets and risks and shows whether controls keep working within the organization's risk tolerance, so it can act quickly when they fall short.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 Risk Management Framework
findings: The framework steps are categorize, select and implement controls, assess, authorize, and monitor continuously.
Controls can be system-specific, common across systems, or hybrid, with accountability for inherited controls.

sources.title: PCI SSC Glossary
findings: The cardholder data environment is the people, processes, and system components that store, process, or transmit cardholder data or sensitive authentication data, plus components with unrestricted connectivity to them.
Segmentation separates systems that handle cardholder data from those that do not.
A targeted risk analysis is a risk analysis for one requirement, used where the requirement allows flexibility (such as frequency) or where the customized approach must show the objective is met.
sources.limits: The glossary points to the standard's appendices for compensating controls and the customized approach instead of defining them.

sources.title: Just Published: PCI DSS v4.0.1
findings: PCI DSS v4.0.1 is a limited revision that adds a customized approach objective under Requirement 3 and does not change the effective date of the future-dated requirements (31 March 2025).
Version 4.0 retired on 31 December 2024.

sources.title: PCI SSC FAQ 1220: official validation documentation
findings: A compliance certificate is not accepted as proof of PCI DSS validation; only the official ROC, AOC, SAQ, and ASV attestation templates are.
An organization using other documents must also be able to give the same information on the official forms.

sources.title: PCI SSC FAQ 1331: SAQ eligibility and requirement applicability
findings: SAQs are reporting tools for merchants under set conditions; payment brands and acquirers may add rules.
SAQ eligibility criteria should not guide which requirements apply in a Report on Compliance unless the compliance-accepting entity reviewed and agreed to it.
sources.limits: One FAQ; it does not define scope.

sources.title: TISAX Participant Handbook
findings: Assessment levels set how deeply an auditor checks: AL 1 only checks that a self-assessment exists, AL 2 adds a plausibility check, evidence review, and an interview, AL 3 adds on-site verification and observation.
Assessment objectives, chosen by the partner's data type, decide which ISA requirements apply and map to a level.
The assessment scope lies within the ISMS scope and may be smaller.
sources.limits: Only the first 100000 characters of the page were read.

sources.title: ENX: Information Security Assessment (ISA)
findings: The ISA is the requirements catalog behind TISAX, maintained by ENX and published by VDA; versions are yearly from 2027, with assessments ordered in a year using that year's version.
sources.limits: Page does not describe levels or catalog structure.

sources.title: ENX: TISAX
findings: TISAX is a shared automotive framework for verifying an organization's information security management; labels reflect objectives such as information security, data protection, or prototype protection and are valid for three years.
Assessment depth varies with the required protection level.
sources.limits: Results are shared in the ENX portal, not public.

sources.title: Cybersecurity Certification Framework (ENISA)
findings: Under the Cybersecurity Act (Regulation (EU) 2019/881), EU certification is a formal evaluation of ICT products, services, or processes by an independent accredited body against defined criteria, ending in a certificate of conformance.
Each EU scheme specifies one or more assurance levels (basic, substantial, high), chosen by the risk of the intended use.
EUCC, for ICT products and based on Common Criteria, is published; EUCS (cloud), EU5G, and others are under development.
sources.limits: Overview page of the EU framework; scheme details live in the implementing acts and scheme documents, which were not fetched.
